questions.question: In which species does nitrogen have an oxidation number of +3? A: NO3-; B: NO2-; C: N2O4; D: NH2OH
questions.answer: B: NO2-
steps: In NO2- the overall charge is -1 and each O is -2, so N + 2(-2) = -1, giving N = +3.
A is wrong: in NO3- N + 3(-2) = -1, so N is +5.
C is wrong: in N2O4 each N is +4. D is wrong: in NH2OH, N + 3(+1) + (-2) = 0, so N is -1.

questions.question: In which reaction is the same element both oxidised and reduced? A: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2; B: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2; C: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2; D: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2
steps: In H2O2 oxygen is -1. In H2O it is -2 (reduced) and in O2 it is 0 (oxidised), so oxygen disproportionates.
A is wrong: zinc is oxidised and hydrogen is reduced, two different elements.
C is wrong: chlorine is reduced and bromine is oxidised. D is wrong: no oxidation numbers change.

questions.question: Give the systematic name, including the oxidation number, of (i) NaClO and (ii) K2Cr2O7.
questions.answer: (i) sodium chlorate(I); (ii) potassium dichromate(VI)
steps: (i) sodium chlorate(I)
(ii) potassium dichromate(VI)
accept: sodium oxochlorate(I) for NaClO
oxidation numbers written in Arabic numerals, e.g. sodium chlorate(1), potassium dichromate(6)

questions.question: Sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfate ions in acidic aqueous solution. Write the half-equation for this oxidation.
steps: Correct species: SO2 and H2O on the left, SO4^2- and H+ on the right, balanced for atoms (SO2 + 2H2O -> SO4^2- + 4H+)
2e- on the right-hand side, so that the charges balance (0 on each side)
accept: state symbols included: SO2(g) + 2H2O(l) -> SO4^2-(aq) + 4H+(aq) + 2e-
H3O+ used in place of H+: SO2 + 6H2O -> SO4^2- + 4H3O+ + 2e-

questions.question: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H2O2(aq) -> 2H2O(l) + O2(g). Calculate the volume of oxygen, measured at room temperature and pressure, formed when 50.0 cm^3 of 0.800 mol dm^-3 hydrogen peroxide decomposes completely. [Molar volume of a gas at room temperature and pressure = 24.0 dm^3 mol^-1]

questions.question: Chlorine reacts with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide to make bleach. (a) Write the ionic equation, including state symbols, for this reaction.
questions.answer: Cl2(g) + 2OH-(aq) -> Cl-(aq) + ClO-(aq) + H2O(l)
steps: Cl2 + 2OH- -> Cl- + ClO- + H2O (correct species and balancing)
State symbols correct: Cl2(g), OH-(aq), Cl-(aq), ClO-(aq), H2O(l)
accept: full equation Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaClO + H2O scores the first mark
OCl- written in place of ClO-
multiples of the equation, provided it is balanced

questions.question: Chlorine reacts with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide: Cl2 + 2OH- -> Cl- + ClO- + H2O. (b) Use oxidation numbers to show that this is a disproportionation reaction.
questions.answer: Cl goes from 0 to -1 (reduced) and from 0 to +1 (oxidised)
steps: Oxidation number of Cl is 0 in Cl2, -1 in Cl- (reduction) and +1 in ClO- (oxidation)
The same element (chlorine) is both oxidised and reduced, so the reaction is a disproportionation
accept: oxidation numbers shown on the equation by labelling each species
Cl2 gains one electron per atom to form Cl- and loses one electron per atom to form ClO-

questions.question: When chlorine is passed into hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide, chlorate(V) ions, ClO3-, are formed. (c) Write the half-equation for the oxidation of Cl2 to ClO3- in alkaline solution.
steps: Cl2 + 12OH- -> 2ClO3- + 6H2O (correct species, balanced for atoms)
+10e- on the right-hand side (charge -12 on each side)
accept: state symbols included

questions.question: Using your answer to (c), and the half-equation Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-, deduce the overall ionic equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide, in which ClO3- and Cl- are formed.
questions.answer: 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> ClO3- + 5Cl- + 3H2O
steps: Multiplies the reduction half-equation by 5 (5Cl2 + 10e- -> 10Cl-) and adds the two half-equations, cancelling the 10e-
3Cl2 + 6OH- -> ClO3- + 5Cl- + 3H2O (simplified to the lowest whole numbers)
accept: 6Cl2 + 12OH- -> 2ClO3- + 10Cl- + 6H2O (not simplified) scores the first mark only
full equation 3Cl2 + 6NaOH -> NaClO3 + 5NaCl + 3H2O

questions.question: A cell is made from a Zn2+(aq)|Zn(s) half-cell, E = -0.76 V, and an Ag+(aq)|Ag(s) half-cell, E = +0.80 V, both under standard conditions. What is the standard e.m.f. of the cell? A: +0.04 V; B: +1.56 V; C: +2.36 V; D: -1.56 V
steps: E cell = E(positive electrode) - E(negative electrode) = +0.80 - (-0.76) = +1.56 V.
A is wrong: it subtracts the magnitudes, 0.80 - 0.76, ignoring the sign of the zinc potential.
C is wrong: it doubles the silver value, wrongly scaling E by the number of electrons. D is wrong: it subtracts the more positive value from the less positive.

questions.question: The half-cell Ag+(aq) + e- <=> Ag(s) is set up under standard conditions. Which change makes its electrode potential less positive? A: using a larger silver electrode; B: dissolving more silver nitrate in the solution; C: adding aqueous sodium chloride to the solution; D: cleaning the silver electrode with emery paper
questions.answer: C: adding aqueous sodium chloride to the solution
steps: Adding Cl-(aq) precipitates AgCl, which lowers [Ag+(aq)].
The equilibrium Ag+ + e- <=> Ag shifts left, so the electrode becomes less positive.
A and D are wrong: electrode size and surface have no effect on E. B is wrong: raising [Ag+] makes E more positive.

questions.question: Describe the standard hydrogen electrode, stating the conditions that make it a standard electrode.
questions.answer: Pt electrode (coated in platinum black) in 1.00 mol dm^-3 H+(aq), with H2 gas at 100 kPa bubbled over it, at 298 K; E is defined as 0 V
steps: Platinum (inert) electrode, coated with platinum black, dipping into the solution
H+(aq) at a concentration of 1.00 mol dm^-3, with hydrogen gas at 100 kPa bubbled over the electrode
Temperature 298 K; the electrode potential of the SHE is defined as 0.00 V

temperature of 25 degrees C
concentration of H+ given as 1 M or 1 mol per dm^3
hydrochloric or sulfuric acid named as the source of H+(aq)

questions.question: The standard electrode potentials are: Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- <=> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O, E = +1.33 V; Cl2 + 2e- <=> 2Cl-, E = +1.36 V. (i) Calculate E cell for the reaction of acidified dichromate(VI) ions with chloride ions, and state whether the reaction is feasible under standard conditions. (ii) Suggest why chlorine can nevertheless be made by heating dichromate(VI) with concentrated hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: (i) E cell = -0.03 V, not feasible under standard conditions; (ii) the high [H+] and [Cl-] change the electrode potentials so that E cell becomes positive
steps: E cell is negative, so the reaction is not feasible under standard conditions
Concentrated HCl has a high [H+] and a high [Cl-]: the higher [H+] makes the dichromate E more positive and the higher [Cl-] makes the Cl2/Cl- E less positive, so E cell becomes positive
accept: E cell is only just negative (-0.03 V), so a change in concentration is enough to make it positive
applying Le Chatelier's principle to Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6Cl- -> 2Cr3+ + 3Cl2 + 7H2O: high [H+] and [Cl-] shift the equilibrium to the right
chlorine gas leaves the mixture, which keeps the reaction moving to the right
heating provides energy to overcome a high activation energy

questions.question: A reaction has a positive E cell under standard conditions but no change is seen when the reagents are mixed. Give two reasons why the reaction may not occur.
questions.answer: High activation energy so the rate is very slow; conditions are not standard (concentration, temperature)
steps: The activation energy is high, so the reaction is too slow at room temperature (kinetically stable)
The conditions are not standard (concentrations, temperature or pressure differ), so the electrode potentials change
accept: E cell is only slightly positive, so a small change in conditions can reverse its sign
no catalyst is present to provide an alternative route with a lower activation energy
concentration of the ions is not 1.00 mol dm^-3

questions.question: The standard electrode potentials are: Ni2+(aq) + 2e- <=> Ni(s), E = -0.25 V; Ag+(aq) + e- <=> Ag(s), E = +0.80 V. For the cell made from these half-cells (i) write the conventional cell diagram, (ii) calculate E cell, and (iii) write the overall equation for the cell reaction.
questions.answer: (i) Ni(s) | Ni2+(aq) || Ag+(aq) | Ag(s); (ii) +1.05 V; (iii) Ni + 2Ag+ -> Ni2+ + 2Ag
steps: Ni(s) | Ni2+(aq) || Ag+(aq) | Ag(s), with nickel (the more negative half-cell) on the left
Ni + 2Ag+ -> Ni2+ + 2Ag (Ni oxidised, Ag+ reduced; the potential is not doubled)
accept: state symbols in the overall equation: Ni(s) + 2Ag+(aq) -> Ni2+(aq) + 2Ag(s)
1.05 V accepted without the plus sign, if the working is correct
dashed or dotted vertical lines for the phase boundaries

questions.question: A student builds a cell from a zinc electrode in 1.00 mol dm^-3 zinc sulfate solution and a copper electrode in 1.00 mol dm^-3 copper(II) sulfate solution. The standard electrode potentials are Zn2+ + 2e- <=> Zn, E = -0.76 V and Cu2+ + 2e- <=> Cu, E = +0.34 V. (a) Name a suitable solution for the salt bridge and explain why a salt bridge is needed.
questions.answer: Potassium nitrate solution; it completes the circuit by allowing ions to move between the half-cells without reacting with either solution
steps: Potassium nitrate solution (a solution of ions which do not react with either half-cell)
Completes the circuit by allowing ions to flow between the half-cells, balancing the charge in each
accept: potassium chloride solution, because neither Zn2+ nor Cu2+ forms an insoluble chloride
potassium sulfate solution
strip of filter paper soaked in the salt solution
allows charge to balance as Zn2+ forms and Cu2+ is used up

questions.question: In the cell in (a), Zn2+ + 2e- <=> Zn has E = -0.76 V and Cu2+ + 2e- <=> Cu has E = +0.34 V. (b) Calculate E cell and state the direction of electron flow in the external circuit.
questions.answer: E cell = +1.10 V; electrons flow from the zinc electrode to the copper electrode
steps: Zinc has the more negative potential, so it is oxidised: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-. This makes zinc the negative electrode.
Electrons flow through the external wire from the negative zinc electrode to the positive copper electrode, where Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.

questions.question: The copper half-cell in (a) is changed so that [Cu2+(aq)] = 0.010 mol dm^-3. The zinc half-cell is unchanged. (c) Predict, with a reason, how E cell changes.
questions.answer: E cell decreases (becomes smaller than +1.10 V)
steps: Lowering [Cu2+] shifts the equilibrium Cu2+ + 2e- <=> Cu to the left, so the copper electrode potential is less positive than +0.34 V
E cell decreases (it becomes smaller than +1.10 V)
accept: the tendency of Cu2+ to be reduced decreases
fewer Cu2+ ions are available to accept electrons
E cell falls but remains positive, because copper is still the positive electrode

questions.question: A student measures the e.m.f. of the cell in (a) using a voltmeter. (d) Explain why a voltmeter of very high resistance is used.
questions.answer: A high-resistance voltmeter draws almost no current, so the reading is the e.m.f. and the cell concentrations do not change
steps: A voltmeter of high resistance draws almost no current from the cell
So the concentrations stay at their standard values (the cell is not discharged) and the reading equals the e.m.f.
accept: no potential difference is lost across the internal resistance of the cell
the cell stays close to equilibrium, so the maximum voltage is measured
otherwise reactions at the electrodes change the concentrations during the measurement

questions.question: A direct methanol fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte has the overall reaction 2CH3OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 4H2O. How many electrons are transferred through the external circuit for each molecule of methanol that reacts? A: 2; B: 4; C: 6; D: 12
steps: The oxidation number of carbon is -2 in CH3OH (C + 3(+1) + (-2) + (+1) = 0) and +4 in CO2, so each carbon atom loses 6 electrons: CH3OH + H2O -> CO2 + 6H+ + 6e-.
A is wrong: 2 electrons per molecule would oxidise methanol only as far as methanal, HCHO. B is wrong: 4 is the number of electrons accepted by each O2 molecule, O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O.
D is wrong: 12 electrons are transferred for the 2 molecules of methanol in the equation as written.

questions.question: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which statement is correct? A: sodium forms at the cathode; B: hydrogen forms at the cathode and the solution becomes alkaline; C: oxygen forms at the anode; D: the pH of the solution falls
questions.answer: B: hydrogen forms at the cathode and the solution becomes alkaline
steps: At the cathode water is reduced in preference to Na+: 2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH-, so OH- builds up and the solution becomes alkaline.
A is wrong: Na+ has a very negative electrode potential and is not discharged from aqueous solution.
C is wrong: the high concentration of Cl- means chlorine is formed at the anode. D is wrong: the pH rises as OH- accumulates.

questions.question: Molten magnesium bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. State the product at each electrode and write a half-equation for each.
questions.answer: Cathode: magnesium, Mg2+ + 2e- -> Mg; anode: bromine, 2Br- -> Br2 + 2e-
steps: Cathode (negative): Mg2+ + 2e- -> Mg
Anode (positive): 2Br- -> Br2 + 2e-
Products identified: magnesium at the cathode and bromine at the anode
accept: state symbols included: Mg2+(l) + 2e- -> Mg(l) and 2Br-(l) -> Br2(g) + 2e-
Br- -> 1/2Br2 + e- accepted
bromine observed as an orange-brown vapour; magnesium forms as a molten metal

questions.question: A vehicle powered by a direct methanol fuel cell uses 4.00 kg of methanol on a journey. The overall reaction is 2CH3OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 4H2O. steps: From 2CH3OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 4H2O, moles of CO2 = moles of CH3OH = 125 mol.

questions.question: An ethanol fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. At the negative electrode, ethanol reacts with water to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions. At the positive electrode, oxygen is reduced to water. Write (i) the half-equation for the reaction at the negative electrode, (ii) the half-equation for the reaction at the positive electrode, and (iii) the overall equation for the cell reaction.
steps: C2H5OH + 3H2O -> 2CO2 + 12H+ + 12e- (correct species, balanced for atoms)
12e- on the right-hand side, so that the charges balance (0 on each side)
C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O (the positive-electrode equation multiplied by 3 so that the electrons cancel, then H+ and H2O cancelled)
accept: state symbols included, e.g. C2H5OH(l) + 3H2O(l) -> 2CO2(g) + 12H+(aq) + 12e-
positive-electrode equation written as 1/2O2 + 2H+ + 2e- -> H2O, provided the overall equation is balanced
the half-equations multiplied up to cancel the electrons, e.g. 3O2 + 12H+ + 12e- -> 6H2O
the overall equation is the same as that for the combustion of ethanol

questions.question: A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte is used to power a bus. (a) Write the half-equations for the reactions at the negative and positive electrodes.

questions.question: In the fuel cell, the electrode potentials are 2H+ + 2e- <=> H2, E = 0.00 V and O2 + 4H+ + 4e- <=> 2H2O, E = +1.23 V. (b) Calculate the standard e.m.f. of the cell.

questions.question: A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is used to power a bus, which carries 35.0 kg of hydrogen in its fuel tanks. (c) Calculate the volume that this hydrogen would occupy at room temperature and pressure, and suggest why the hydrogen is not stored at this pressure. [Ar of H = 1.0; molar volume of a gas = 24.0 dm^3 mol^-1]
questions.answer: 4.20 x 10^5 dm^3 (420 m^3); too large to carry, so the hydrogen is compressed (or liquefied)
steps: Mr of H2 = 2.0, so moles of H2 = 35 000 / 2.0 = 17 500 mol.
This volume is far too large to carry on a bus, so the hydrogen has to be stored compressed at high pressure (or liquefied).

questions.question: Hydrogen fuel cells and petrol engines can both power vehicles. (d) Evaluate the use of hydrogen fuel cells, rather than petrol engines, to power road vehicles.
questions.answer: Fuel cells emit only water at the point of use and are more efficient, but hydrogen is hard to store, needs a supply infrastructure, and is only low-carbon if made using renewable energy; overall a benefit only if the hydrogen is produced cleanly
steps: Only water is emitted at the point of use, so no CO2, NOx or particulates from the vehicle
Higher efficiency than a petrol engine, because chemical energy is converted directly into electrical energy
Hydrogen is difficult to store: a gas needing high pressure or very low temperature, with a low energy density by volume, and flammable
Few hydrogen refuelling stations, and fuel cells use expensive catalysts such as platinum
Hydrogen is mostly made from natural gas (producing CO2), or by electrolysis which needs electricity, so the benefit depends on how it is made
A reasoned conclusion, e.g. cleaner at the point of use but only worthwhile with low-carbon hydrogen and better storage and supply
accept: quiet, with few moving parts so lower maintenance
refuelling is quick compared with recharging a battery
hydrogen leaks are invisible and risk an explosion
fuel cell stacks degrade and need replacing over time
range comparable with a petrol vehicle
